item.title: Ethiopia is slipping into a war again that could expand to more countries
item.description: The conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.
item.content:encoded:
Four years after a fragile ceasefire ended widespread conflict in Ethiopia, the region is again slipping back into full-out war.

On September 23, 2026, advancing soldiers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front seized government positions in northern Ethiopia.

It followed the announcement of a new alliance of seven armed movements in opposition to the Ethiopian government and deteriorating relations between the country and neighboring Eritrea, which it accuses of supporting the new alliance.

As an expert on conflict in the Horn of Africa and Ethiopian national security, I know the spiraling conditions now have been long in the making.

The November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement ended immediate fighting between Ethiopia and Tigrayan rebels, but it did not constitute a comprehensive peace settlement. Crucially, it was never followed by wider political negotiations to address the root causes of the war. The concern now is that the conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.

How has the conflict escalated?

The September 23 ground offensive by the TPLF drew global attention to the situation in Ethiopia. But in reality, the ratcheting up of tensions between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the TPLF has been going on for months.

item.title: 11 Indians injured in attack on ship in Strait of Hormuz
item.description: The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, the Ministry of External Affairs said.
item.content:encoded:
Eleven Indians were injured in an attack on a commercial ship while passing through the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Oman, on Tuesday, the Ministry of External Affairs said.

The projectile hit the Panama-flagged MT On Peace, which had 19 crew members on board, including 17 Indians. Twelve people were injured in the attack.

The injured were evacuated with the help of Omani authorities and are undergoing treatment.

The incident came days after an Indian seafarer was killed in an attack on a commercial ship off the coast of Oman on September 23. The vessel was sailing towards India when two torpedoes struck the ship.

Eleven Indian seafarers have been killed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in West Asia began, in attacks involving four Indian ships and 60 foreign-flagged vessels.

The ministry condemned Tuesday’s attack and said that such incidents remained a cause of “deep concern” for India.

“We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region,” it said.

The ministry added: “The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, and navigation and commerce through international waterways must be restored at the earliest.”

item.title: Bangladesh measles outbreak claims 900 lives – and serves as warning for why vaccination matters
item.description: Even a small dip in vaccination rates can leave pockets of unprotected children.
item.content:encoded:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the Covid pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.

“Gita Miss is giving us so much work,” complained Sumi.

“Yeah, all because of that awful cyclone,” said Moyna. “We missed so many school days. Now we have to catch up fast.”

“Enough talking, you two!” Biswas Sir said, shaking his head. “Always stuck together like glue, chattering about something or the other.”

He started reviewing tenths and hundredths. The kids groaned in unison when Biswas Sir said, “A frog is 30.5 centimetres long – now who can tell me what that is in centimetres and millimetres?”

item.description: The negotiations have reached a point beyond which additional give and ​take would be ‘very, very difficult’, the Union finance minister said.
item.content:encoded:
Trade deal talks between India and the United States have reached a “plateau” and further concessions might be difficult, Reuters quoted Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman as saying on Monday.

Sitharaman blamed the increasing use of tariffs by the US for the stalled trade talks. She said that Washington was “weaponising” tariffs.

After an interim trade deal was agreed upon on February 2, US tariffs on Indian goods would have been reduced to 18% from a combined rate of 50%. The earlier rate of 50% had included a punitive levy of 25% imposed in August 2025 over India’s purchase of Russian oil.

However, negotiations on the final deal were hampered after the US Supreme Court on February 20 struck down global tariffs imposed by Trump, ruling that he had exceeded his authority.

In response, Trump imposed a temporary 10% tariff on goods imported into the US, citing his authority under the 1974 Trade Act. This has left the status of US’ trade deals with countries, including India, unclear.

item.title: Francis Halzen awarded physics Nobel for discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
item.description: His ‘vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental’ for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Physics was on Tuesday awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin and his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

Halzen, 82, is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States.

“His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

The observatory is near the South Pole in Antarctica. Using the observatory, researchers “can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”, the academy added.

Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the glacial ice.

He will receive a prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was jointly awarded to three scientists – Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth – for their research on brain activity.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

Kabir had won both Rejinagar and Nowda in the May Assembly elections. He retained Nowda.

Kabir had been having arguments with the police since polling began, alleging that a large number of personnel had been deployed near his home and at polling booths to intimidate voters and his party workers, The Hindu reported.

The police arrived at the party office and asked Kabir to leave, saying that he could not remain there during polling as he was neither a candidate nor an authorised polling agent.

As Ava sinks, the surface is farther away. It is the memory of a day from fifty years ago. Why do the worst moments repeat themselves like a knife to the heart? Why is she being punished for what happened to Roxanne? Must I not love my children? I did once. But at the end of our life, we need them to do more than run the house. We need them to be happy. item.title: Maharashtra to cut water supply by 10% amid drought, El Niño concerns
item.description: The measure will be in force from October 16 till August 31, said the state water resources minister.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra government on Monday announced a minimum 10% water cut in all urban areas from October 16, citing a “significant decrease in rainfall” caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon.

The El Niño weather phenomenon involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to reduced monsoon rainfall in India.

In September, the Maharashtra government had declared drought conditions in 74% of the state’s subdistricts amid a deficit in rainfall during the southwest monsoon season.

On Monday, state Minister of Water Resources Girish Mahajan said that the department has issued directives to use water with “extreme frugality and implement stringent measures”. He added that top priority has been given to ensure preventing any shortage of drinking water.

The new water strategy will be in force until August 31, said Mahajan, adding that effects of the El Niño are likely to last into the coming year.

The state government’s plan also outlines the need to curb water leakage and ensure that sewage treatment plants are operated at full capacity.

Water for irrigation will be allocated only after meeting the requirements for drinking water, livestock and fodder, according to the plan.

item.title: The world order is ‘complicated’. Can Indian foreign policy navigate ‘situationships’?
item.description: New Delhi’s global posturing has always coexisted with a pragmatic practice closer to home.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s much-discussed special address at Davos in January called for a world of “values-based realism.” First proposed by Finland’s President, Alexander Stubb, values-based realism describes not a strategy, but an “instrument – temporary, adaptive, and situational…that espouses values while engaging respectfully with those who do not share them.”

Put more colloquially, this macro-geopolitical landscape operates exactly like a Gen Z “situationship” – relationships that are not beholden to labels, exclusivity, and can be non-committal.

India, with its cautious diplomatic language and history of moral rhetoric on the global stage, may not seem like a player suited to this new world of “situationships.” Yet New Delhi’s record navigating problematic regimes in its own neighborhoods suggests that India may actually enter this new order with more experience than most.

Situationships and values-based realism

Where once the rules-based international order was the organising principle for global affairs, the broader strategic framework increasingly gaining traction is values-based realism, which underscores the rising salience of variable, issue-by-issue geometries that form when states choose immediate interests over long-term normative alignment.

item.title: Missives from the heart: When Hindi cinema put the letter to song
item.description: From flowers tucked into envelopes and lovers who needed postmen to write for them, Hindi films knew that a letter could carry much more than a message.

Historians spend a surprising amount of time reading other people’s letters. Love letters, family letters, petitions, complaints, advice, requests for money, quarrels between husbands and wives, messages written from prison or pardes. There are khat, chitthi, patra, paati, sandesa and paigham. There are envelopes and postcards, postmen and pigeons, letters dictated to someone else, letters carrying flowers, letters from home and letters that never arrive. Some are read. Some are sung. Archer died “suddenly and peacefully at his home between writing sessions”, said the publisher.

Author of 31 novels, he had sold more than 30 crore copies of his books worldwide. His final book, Adam and Eve, was scheduled to be published on Tuesday.

item.title: A new book examines why rural women are undergoing sterilisation despite ambivalence about surgery
item.description: An excerpt from ‘State Intimacies: Sterilization, Care and Reproductive Chronicity in Rural North India’, by Eva Fiks.

While wider biomedical discourses focus on the laparoscope’s convenience, rural women often resist this simplistic understanding and draw on their everyday lives to develop an understanding of how this technology works. The way that the laparoscope enters everyday conversations of rural Rajasthani women – what it is, how it works and whether it is better than open surgery – uncovers women’s relationships with population control efforts, the fascination with technology, and power exercised by the state and biomedical institutions. The relationship between women and laparoscopes encapsulates the reasons why tubal ligation is seen by some people as a technologically sophisticated option that is implemented by “choice”, in contrast to the widespread concerns about the quality of care and numerous women’s deaths in sterilisation camps in a population control programme often described as a form of violence against women.

Across India, tubal ligation is often referred to as an operation. Women in my field site often specify what type of operation they have had: open surgery or a laparoscopic tubectomy. They refer to open surgery as bara (big) operation, tankewala (with stitches) operation or hathwala (done by hand) operation. item.title: How El Niño is causing droughts in parts of the world and floods elsewhere
item.description: It is a result of climactic conditions being shaped by the warming Pacific Ocean and the air above it.
item.content:encoded:
The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year’s El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

El Niño, the warm phase of a natural fluctuation in the Earth’s climate system, can reshape weather thousands of miles away, bringing drought to some regions while increasing the risk of heavy rain and flooding in others. To understand why, you need to follow what happens to the Pacific’s warm water – and the air above it.

Usually, winds over the tropical Pacific blow from east to west, pushing warm surface water towards the western Pacific, where it piles up around Indonesia and nearby regions. These are the trade winds. As warm water moves westward, colder water from deeper in the ocean rises to replace it in the east – a process called upwelling. This is why the western Pacific is usually much warmer than the eastern Pacific.

item.title: Scabies: The invisible skin infection that is more than skin-deep
item.description: A series on health conditions that disproportionately affects marginalised communities.
item.content:encoded:
What is it like to itch all the time, to lose sleep every night, to be dazed in the classroom and accept this as normal?

For many months now, 12-year-old Budhram’s* skin had been itching incessantly. Three of the ten boys in his dormitory at a residential school for Baiga Adivasis (a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group) in Chattisgarh had the same problem. Back home, Budhram’s younger siblings and mother also had an itch that refused to go away.

This story of daily, mass torment is common across India – from Kondh tribals in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh to the labouring poor of Bihar and Gujarat. Entire villages may have a disease that has afflicted humanity for millenia, but remains neglected by patients and public health authorities alike – scabies.

Some local practitioners’ injections provide only partial relief, at a high recurring cost. item.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine awarded to three scientists for brain research
item.description: One American and two German researchers won the honour for ‘laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience’.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was on Monday jointly awarded to three scientists for their work on light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

Peter Hegemann from Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg in Germany discovered a protein, named channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga.

Karl Deisseroth from The Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University in the United States developed a way to turn the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.

Their research has fundamentally changed the way science understands the human brain, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said in a statement. The three scientists have “laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience”, it added.

Their research has led to the discovery of a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the brain, the Nobel Assembly said.

Researchers are using the method to try and restore eyesight in people.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, the chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.

The three scientists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

item.title: Can a messy person change or are some people just naturally tidier?
item.description: Personality isn’t destiny and changing patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.
item.content:encoded:
Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the wardrobe, and their kitchen bench remains mysteriously visible.

Others can clean the house on Sunday and wonder by Wednesday how everything became messy again.

It’s tempting to explain this as personality: “I’m just a messy person.” And there is some truth to that. But personality isn’t destiny. Our surroundings and the small things we repeatedly do within them matter too.

In fact, changing those patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.

Are some people just naturally tidier?

Psychologists describe personality in terms of relatively enduring patterns in how people tend to think, feel and behave.

One of the “Big Five” personality traits is conscientiousness. It includes tendencies towards being industrious, self-controlled and orderly. So, someone higher in conscientiousness – particularly its orderliness aspects – may find keeping things organised easier.

But “relatively enduring” doesn’t mean personality is fixed.

Large studies following people over time show personality is both stable and changeable. For example, people tend to become more conscientious during different stages of adulthood, such as when they have children or new responsibilities.

So, saying “I’m a messy person” may describe a tendency. It doesn’t condemn you to a lifetime of losing your keys.

I don’t need any of them. I certainly can’t afford them. Thankfully, they’ll never arrive.

Instead of Amazon, I spent the past week browsing a new breed of websites known as “dopamine sites,” a trend that emerged in South Korea. These websites – like Dopamine Shop and FoodNeverComes – recreate the entire ritual of online shopping: You search for products, compare reviews, add items to your cart, enter a shipping address, place an order, and even track your delivery.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: A century after Gandhi described the four pillars of swaraj, how do they hold up?
item.description: He pressed for equal rights for Dalits, women and minorities, an economic model that is equitable and sustainable, and the cultivation of non-violence.
item.content:encoded:
Mahatma Gandhi spent the last three decades of his life battling for his country’s freedom from British colonial rule. In this time, he rarely wrote or spoke about what he felt a free India should look like. However, in March 1922, he offered a short, succinct definition of swaraj that is worth revisiting today. Here is what he said:

“Removal of untouchability, manufacture of khaddar, Hindu-Muslim unity, cultivation of non-violence are not measures of a temporary nature. They are the four pillars on which the structure of swaraj must for ever rest. Take away any one of them and it must topple down.”

Let us unpack this statement and gloss each of its four elements.

We may take “removal of untouchability” to stand more broadly for the pursuit of social justice, which of course includes removing not just the inequalities of caste but also of gender. Unlike the other savarna leaders of the Congress – Nehru, Patel, Bose, et al – Gandhi was keenly aware of how the prevalence of untouchability undermined the Indian case for freedom. He therefore called it a “sin”, and those who practised it the “Dyers of Hinduism”.

Sunday Adeniyi Adegeye, known as King Sunny Adé, is 80 this year. He has devoted more than 60 years of his life to influencing Nigeria’s popular music and promoting the unique sounds of jùjú music.

Jùjú is a Nigerian musical tradition that combines intricate rhythms, percussion, guitars, talking drums, call-and-response and Yoruba oral culture. It’s not only entertainment but a vehicle for expressing cultural identity, transmitting proverbs and praise traditions, and social life commentary.

Sunny Adé’s career embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim. From his beginnings in Lagos to his rise as the globally celebrated “King of Jùjú”, his story is intertwined with the development of contemporary African popular music.

As a social philosopher, I regard Sunny Adé’s music as a tool for social change. This is because it transforms cultural expression into a medium of moral reflection and social engagement. His music communicates values such as communal responsibility, respect, humility, peace, diligence and integrity. It also draws attention to the social problems confronting Nigerian society.

I’ve argued that Sunny Adé’s music addresses social challenges, preserves Yoruba identity and promotes civic awareness, national unity and moral renewal.

The houses being broken into belonged to wealthy families who had abandoned them during the plague of 1896-’97. For some time, the police had no idea who was responsible. item.description: He helped build the legal ground for the Mahad Satyagraha and ended his career as president of the Hindu Mahasabha.
item.content:encoded:
On 4 August 1924, Sitaram Keshav Bole moved a resolution in the Bombay Legislative Council granting untouchables access to public water bodies, wells, dharmashalas, schools, courts and hospitals. Three years later, it was this resolution that was invoked by BR Ambedkar, a lawyer who would go on to lead India’s Dalit rights movement, as he led thousands of so-called untouchables to Mahad to drink water from a public water tank that had been barred to them.

The Mahad satyagraha was a critical moment in the anti-caste movement – a movement whose young leader, Ambedkar, had been mentored by Bole since 1907.

Just over a decade later, in 1938, Bole – a man who had worked for decades on behalf of underprivileged castes and classes – became president of the Bombay Provincial Hindu Mahasabha, a Hindu nationalist organisation. This contradiction at the heart of Bole’s life has gone almost entirely unexamined.

Since branches were established in Maharashtra from 1923, the Hindu Mahasabha there had been dominated by Brahmins. Its politics centred on the challenges its leaders perceived from other religions, particularly Islam. Among the questions the Supreme Court has asked the high-powered enquiry committee to answer on the Cockroach Janata Party protest crackdown, one has received more attention than others: did the police use “excessive force and violence” against protesters at Jantar Mantar on July 20?

The question undoubtedly merits attention. Going by the accounts of the petitioners, witnesses and human rights bodies, the clampdown was ferocious. Apart from batons and tear gas, the police allegedly used nail-studded lathis, rubber bullets, electric batons and even pellet guns. A Human Rights Watch report quotes a 24-year-old photojournalist as saying, “I have photos of protesters just standing there and the police beating them.”

item.title: ‘Delhi was a warzone, Mumbai a concert’: Protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar strike contrasting notes

A few hours into the Gandhi Jayanti protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and Mumbai’s Shivaji Park to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the contrast in the mood at each venue could not have been more stark.

Instagram commentator Oamkaar put it succinctly. “Delhi is a warzone,” he noted. “Mumbai is a concert.”

What united protestors in each city, though, was their anger against Kumar, whom they held responsible for the chaotic Special Intensive Revision of the voters’ rolls that has resulted in millions of citizens across the country being deleted from the lists.

Since the exercise began in June 2025, there have been concerns that the SIR could deny genuine electors their right to vote and shape election outcomes.

item.title: Nutrients in food mimic calorie restrictions. Can they improve our health?
item.description: Research in humans has yet to show that compounds reproduce the effects of calorie restriction or extend healthspan.
item.content:encoded:
Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

Researchers often use the term healthspan for the years spent in good health, free from disability or chronic disease. In 2021, global life expectancy was 71.4 years, while healthy life expectancy was 61.9 years, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). That represents a gap of nine and a half years. A separate analysis estimated that this gap widened in 203 of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.

The WHO takes a broader view of healthy ageing, focusing on the abilities that allow people to do what they value, such as undertaking daily tasks, maintaining relationships and contributing to society. This recognises that people can live well while managing a health condition. “Functional healthspan” describes how long someone maintains the capacities needed for independent living.

As we age, declining muscle strength and mass, reduced aerobic fitness and even “inflammaging” (or low-grade inflammation) become more prevalent. These changes vary considerably between people. Diet, physical activity and sleep can influence how well we age, although income, housing, healthcare and the wider environment also play important roles.

item.title: Mumbai: Six allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants arrested
item.description: They have been accused of providing forged Aadhaar and other identity documents to Bangladeshi citizens to help them enter India.
item.content:encoded:
Six allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi migrants were arrested in Mumbai, ANI quoted the police as saying on Friday.

The six persons have been accused of providing forged Aadhaar and other identity documents to Bangladeshi citizens to help them enter India, ANI reported.

Forty forged Aadhaar cards, Permanent Account Number cards, railway tickets with QR codes and other Indian identity documents were recovered from them, the news agency quoted the Mumbai Police as saying.

Since the terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam in April 2025, the police in several states, most of them ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party, have been detaining Bengali-speaking persons – mostly Muslims – and asking them to prove that they are Indian citizens.

Several persons have been forced into Bangladesh after they allegedly could not prove their Indian citizenship. In some cases, persons who were mistakenly sent to Bangladesh returned to the country after state authorities in India proved that they were Indians.

Scroll has also reported on several cases of persons who were forced into Bangladesh being brought back to India, as the authorities had failed to follow the process laid down by the Union home ministry for such deportations.

item.title: How ‘new’ is the tilcayo, the first cat species to be discovered in a 100 years?
item.description: Researchers knew of a tiger cat occurred in Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, but it had never been formally described.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have described a species of tiger cat that was previously unknown to science. From Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, it is the first discovery of a living novel cat species in more than 100 years.

The tilcayo (Leopardus tilcayo) takes its species name from the name locals already had for it. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer who discovered the species and co-author of the Current Biology paper that describes it, said the name honors traditional knowledge in the region.

The tilcayo is smaller than a domestic cat at 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds). It has rounded ears, a slender body and a coat with large spots.

“I have the honor of naming a cat, and that’s a really big thing,” Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is also a researcher at the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia, told Mongabay by phone.

For decades, researchers lumped small spotted cats across South America under a single species name: Leopardus tigrinus or tiger cat. However, evidence had been mounting for years that the group might contain several species.

In the article published on September 17, researchers unwound the species’ genetic web and confirmed at least four distinct species.

item.title: Punjab: Two arrested for allegedly spreading rumours of girls missing from university hostel
item.description: The two persons who were detained are former students, police said.
item.content:encoded:
The Punjab Police on Friday arrested two persons for allegedly provoking students of Chitkara University to protest by spreading rumours on social media that two women students had gone missing from the institute’s hostel, The Indian Express reported.

The unrest at the private university began on the night of September 25 after rumours circulated on social media that two students had gone missing from their hostel.

The students allegedly damaged two police vehicles and assaulted a police officer during the protest. They also alleged that the officer was under the influence of alcohol when he reached the campus to control the situation.

On Friday, Patiala Senior Superintendent of Police Harmandeep Singh Hans said the arrested persons, Himanshu and Aryan, were former students of the university, The Indian Express reported. They allegedly incited students by spreading misleading messages in multiple social media groups.

They have been booked under sections of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita pertaining to attempt to murder, wrongful confinement, obstructing a public servant, assault on a public servant, criminal intimidation, wrongful restraint, disturbing public peace, rioting, unlawful assembly and criminal conspiracy, the newspaper reported.

The first information report was registered on September 29, and police are trying to apprehend 10 other persons named in the FIR, the officer said.

item.title: The reason for Indian democracy’s downslide is collapse of judiciary: Indira Jaising
item.description: ‘Sons of judges are judges, the judiciary makes no apologies for being dynastic.’
item.content:encoded:
Few people know more about India’s courts than Indira Jaising. In a career spanning more than half a century, Jaising has practised both at the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court.

On this episode of ‘Scroll Adda’, she speaks to Shoaib Daniyal on the ills plaguing the judiciary. Dynasty has taken over the courts, she says, leading to a lack of intellectual development. Bright young lawyers without family contacts are forced to leave litigation.

The judiciary is not doing its job of being a check on the executive. Jaising argues that this government is simply ignoring the Constitution and the courts are unable to stop it. ‘The reason for Indian democracy’s downslide is the collapse of the judiciary,’ she says.

Meanwhile, public movements like the Jantar Mantar protests, sparked by the Chief Justice’s “cockroach” comment, show that anger against the judiciary is boiling over into the streets.

item.title: ‘Nothing imminent’: US official on trade deal with India
item.description: Jamieson Greer said Donald Trump and Narendra Modi may have another phone call soon to assess the progress on the negotiations.
item.content:encoded:
United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Thursday said that India and the US were nearing the end of negotiations for a trade deal, but added that an agreement was not imminent as the two sides had identified a “universe of items that are sticking points”, ANI reported.

“We are continually trying to finish the trade deal with India…,” he said.

Greer’s remarks came a day after he met Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal during the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The US is hosting the G20 this year.

Greer described his conversation with Goyal as “very constructive”.

“At the same time, I do not think there is something imminent, but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points,” ANI quoted him as saying. “We are working diligently towards them.”

Greer also said US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi could speak again “very soon” to assess progress of the trade deal.

On Wednesday, Modi and Trump reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation, including trade, defence, energy and critical technologies, the Ministry of External Affairs said.

item.content:encoded:
A Hindu religious group whose visit to the Eiffel Tower last month triggered a controversy said on Thursday that an investigation had established that it did not ask for women staff to be removed from the Paris landmark.

The statement came after the General Inspectorate of the City of Paris found that there had been “no explicit request” from the delegation to remove women, AFP reported.

On September 7, staff at the monument went on a brief strike to protest the removal of women colleagues during the BAPS delegation visit, two days earlier.

The removal of the women staff sparked criticism from French politicians across the political spectrum, who said the country’s commitment to gender equality was non-negotiable.

On Tuesday, the company that manages the Eiffel Tower said its chief would step down in the wake of the controversy.

Patrick Branco Ruivo will leave his role at the end of the year after an internal probe found “operational flaws and shortcomings” in organising the visit that had led to the “unacceptable” removal of women staff.

Eiffel Tower employees had alleged that “workplace instructions led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and rendered invisible on the basis of their gender” during the delegation’s visit, PTI reported.

item.title: Geetanjali Shree’s ‘Our City That Year’ is on the Warwick Prize for Women in Translation longlist
item.description: The shortlist will be announced on October 26, and the winner will be announced at a ceremony at in London on 16 November.
item.content:encoded:
Geetanjali Shree’s Our City That Year, translated by Daisy Rockwell from the original 1998 Hindi novel Hamara Shahar Us Baras, is one of the 13 books longlisted for the 10th annual award of the £1000 Warwick Prize for Women in Translation in 2026.

Rockwell and Shree were co-winners of the prize in 2022 for the International Booker Prize winner Tomb of Sand, translated from the original Hindi novel Ret Samadhi (with Osebol: Voices from a Swedish Village by Marit Kapla, translated from the Swedish by Peter Graves).

The prize was established by the University of Warwick in 2017 to address the gender imbalance in translated literature and to increase the number of international women’s voices especially among British and Irish readers.

This year, the competition received a total of 164 eligible entries representing 37 languages, the highest so far. The longlist covers 12 languages and includes fiction, poetry, short stories, and narrative non-fiction. The jury comprises Arifa Akbar, Véronique Tadjo, and Boyd Tonkin.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Tagore: An Illustrated Biography’, by Uma Das Gupta.
item.content:encoded:
In one of his letters to his wife, Mrinalini Devi, Rabindranath wrote:

I do constantly try not to worry about our children. It is our duty to see to it that they are well-behaved and that they get a good education. Beyond that it is a mistake to torture our minds over them. They will grow up to do their life’s work in their own way whether good, bad, or indifferent. They are our children, true, but they are also individual in their own right. We shall not exercise control over the way they live their lives.

Let us do our duty by them but let us not expect too much from them. How they shall turn out as human beings is in God’s hands. Expecting and imagining that my child shall be the best of all is the product of a certain vanity. I have no right to do that. So many other children have hard lives, do we feel concerned for them?
